content: 1. Karlson 2004: This study was a prospective cohort study involving a cohort of 121,700 female nurses aged 30–35 years who were enrolled in the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS) in 1976. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) cases were confirmed through medical record reviews and connective tissue disease screening questionnaires. A total of 674 cases of RA were confirmed between 1976 and 2002. For the analysis of the association between breastfeeding (BF) and RA risk, only 338 patients diagnosed with RA after 1986 (when BF history was reported) were included. Exclusion criteria included women with RA as of June 1976, those with unconfirmed RA diagnoses, non-responders to supplementary RA questionnaires, and women reporting any cancer (except non-melanoma skin cancer) at baseline or during follow-up. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four groups: 3 months, 4–11 months, 12–23 months, and 24 months or more. 2. Kersey 2005: This cross-sectional study surveyed children aged 2–5 years in an outpatient clinic waiting room at an inner-city community health center in Chicago. The survey included questions about breastfeeding, such as whether the child was still breastfeeding. The study did not provide clear information on the risk of bias in the selection of reported results or other potential biases. 3. Ki 2017: This cross-sectional study utilized data from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) conducted between 2010 and 2012. Participants included postmenopausal women, excluding nulliparous women and premenopausal women. Breastfeeding duration per child was calculated by dividing the total breastfeeding period by the number of breastfed children. Participants were divided into four groups based on breastfeeding duration: non-breastfeeders, 1–6 months, 7–12 months, and more than 18 months per child. 4. Kikafunda 1998: This cross-sectional study involved infants and young children aged 0–30 months from Busimbi sub-county in Uganda. Stratified multistage random sampling was used to select households, and 261 children were studied, with 70% from rural areas and 30% from semi-urban areas. A validated, pre-coded questionnaire was administered to mothers in their home settings by trained researchers. The study did not provide clear information on the risk of bias in the selection of reported results or other potential biases. 5. Kim 2015: This retrospective cross-sectional study used data from KNHANES V, conducted in South Korea from 2010 to 2012. Exclusion criteria included premenopausal women, women without childbirth history, and those with secondary causes of osteoporosis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, thyroid disease, or chronic renal failure. Breastfeeding duration was calculated as the total period of breastfeeding divided by the number of breastfed children. 6. Kim 2020a: This prospective cohort study utilized data from the Panel Study on Korean Children (PSKC). Participants were recruited using stratified multistage sampling to represent nationwide household populations. Data on breastfeeding duration and child development were collected through interviews and assessments, including the Korean Ages and Stages Questionnaires (K-ASQ) and the Denver II developmental screening test. 7. Kondolot 2017: This cross-sectional study analyzed data from the Anthropometry of Turkish Children Aged 0–6 Years (ATCA-06) database, collected between September 2009 and May 2010 in Kayseri, Turkey. Children were randomly selected based on family income levels, and exclusion criteria included low birth weight, prematurity, multiple births, chronic diseases, malnutrition, and incomplete records. Parental declarations and medical records were used to complete questionnaires. 8. Krenz-Niedbala 2015: This cross-sectional study involved pupils from 31 randomly selected primary schools in Poznań, Poland. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as less than 3 months, 3–6 months, 7–12 months, and over 12 months. Outcomes included asthma and obesity. The study did not provide clear information on the risk of bias in the selection of reported results or other potential biases. 9. Kvale 1987: This prospective cohort study invited all women aged 20–69 years in four Norwegian counties to participate in a breast cancer screening program between 1956 and 1959. Participants were followed up until 1980. Lactation experience for the first three births and total breastfeeding duration were recorded. Outcomes included breast cancer, cervical cancer, ovarian cancer, and other cancers. 10. Lee 2003: This prospective cohort study included 129,783 Korean government workers who participated in biennial health maintenance physicals conducted by the Korea Medical Insurance Corporation (KMIC) in 1992. A subset of 199,521 premenopausal women aged 20 years and older was enrolled in the Korean Women’s Cohort (KWC) Study in 1994. Exclusion criteria included nulliparous women, those with no lactation information, and women with a cancer diagnosis in 1994. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into periods of 1–12 months or 13–24 months. 11. Lee 2016: This study was part of the MOCEH study, a multi-center prospective birth cohort study. Mothers were asked about breastfeeding duration and formula use at 6and 12-month follow-ups. Participants were categorized into six groups based on breastfeeding duration, ranging from formula feeding only to breastfeeding for 12 months or more. Outcomes included developmental scores assessed using the Korean version of the Bayley Scales of Infant Development II. 12. Li 2020: This cross-sectional study analyzed data from the Zhejiang Aging and Health Cohort Study, which included 5,487 postmenopausal women. Breastfeeding duration was calculated as the total months spent breastfeeding divided by the number of full-term pregnancies. Cognitive impairment was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), with education-specific cut-off scores for cognitive impairment. 13. Lima 2019: This prospective cohort study followed women from the 1982 Pelotas Birth Cohort Study in Brazil. Inclusion criteria required participants to have delivered at least one live birth, not be pregnant at the time of the interview, and have information on breastfeeding duration and at least one cardiovascular risk factor. Breastfeeding duration was calculated as the cumulative lifetime duration of lactation for all offspring. 14. Linhares 2015: This study followed participants from the 1982 Pelotas Birth Cohort Study in Brazil. Mothers were interviewed about maternal and child health, socioeconomic conditions, and pregnancy complications. Participants were followed up multiple times, and in 2012–2013, cohort members were invited to visit the study clinic. 15. Lossius 2018: This prospective cohort study used data from the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study. Pregnant women were recruited nationwide at 18 weeks of gestation. Breastfeeding duration was reported at intervals of 6–8, 9–11, 12–14, and 15–18 months. Breastfeeding was defined as any breastfeeding, regardless of the introduction of solids or formula. The primary outcome was current asthma at 7 years of age, based on prescription data. 16. Luo 2019: This prospective cohort study analyzed data from the Women’s Health Initiative, a large study addressing morbidity and mortality among postmenopausal women. Exclusion criteria included women with a history of cancer (except non-melanoma skin cancer). This summary provides a detailed and professional overview of the studies, their methodologies, and key findings.
